editorial_note: Original Chapter 4 timed self-assessment with technical and ambiguity checks. Independent human review is not claimed. The site adds the fifth uncertainty choice and ten-second timing. These questions do not replace EX016–EX020 or release any translation unit.

questions.prompt: At 09:14, the proposed svc-enroll export is narrow, but the interface offers all identities. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Export all identities now and request permission afterward.
Stop that transfer and seek a permitted narrower method or explicit amendment.
Treat interface access as approval for every available field.
Record C09's later 09:16 approval as already available.

questions.explanation: B preserves scope and the actual decision boundary: the custodian can propose an authorized narrower method or seek a scope amendment. A performs the unapproved transfer first. C confuses technical capability with permission. D imports a later case approval into the 09:14 request. C08's reported expiry prioritizes attention but does not expand authority.
questions.source: Chapter 4, Week 4 / course Day 16, #week-04-day-01, Assumptions and evidence and Worked contrast; EX016.

questions.prompt: C09 records copy receipt at 09:18 but supplies no source object ID, byte count or digest. Which statement is supported?

options.text: The received export is proved complete because it has two visible rows.
The original producer records were all preserved by a source hold.
A case copy was reported received; byte integrity and source completeness remain unverified.
The missing digest proves that the copy was altered.

questions.explanation: C states the observed workflow status without inventing a byte check. A extrapolates from a visible subset to complete source coverage. B substitutes receipt of a copy for an applied source-retention control. D treats an unperformed comparison as a measured mismatch. Missing metadata limits claims; it does not establish that the supplied rows are false.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.2 and §4.E2; Week 4 / course Day 17, #week-04-day-02, case-copy and missing-fields paragraphs; EX017.

questions.prompt: A custodian later supplies a digest absent from the original C09 receipt. How should the record incorporate it?

options.text: Silently add it to the 09:18 receipt as if measured then.
Replace the original receipt and delete its missing-field history.
Use V4's digest so that the original form remains complete.
Add a dated supplement identifying the object, source and actual check status.

questions.explanation: D preserves what was known at receipt and records the later information with its actual provenance. A backdates knowledge and measurement. B erases the earlier evidence-quality gap. C substitutes unrelated classroom bytes for an unknown export. A supplied digest and an independently recomputed comparison are also different observations and must retain separate statuses.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.E4, manifest supplement paragraph; Week 4 / course Day 17, #week-04-day-02, Custody mechanism; EX017.

questions.prompt: The V4 program reproduces its expected 34-byte count and SHA-256 digest. What does that establish about C09?

options.text: No C09 byte verification; the result concerns the separate V4 fixture.
C09 contains exactly those 34 bytes.
C09's two events are authentic producer records.
C09's complete collection scope and authority are proved.

questions.explanation: A identifies the tested object: V4 is artificial local data, not the missing C09 CSV bytes. B invents byte identity between different objects. C turns fixture reproducibility into producer authentication. D turns a checksum into scope and permission evidence. The measured result is useful only with its actual object and comparison boundary.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.4 and §4.8; Week 4 / course Day 18, #week-04-day-03, Worked contrast; EX018.

questions.prompt: W4-BYTES shows equal splitlines() results for its LF and CRLF representations. Which comparison result is also true?

options.text: Their raw bytes and digests must match because the lines look equal.
Both representations have the same 34-byte length.
Their lengths are 34 and 36; raw bytes and tested digests differ.
The difference proves intentional tampering with C09.

questions.explanation: C matches the executed fixture: replacing two LF terminators with CRLF adds two bytes, while splitlines() removes the terminators from its returned lines. A confuses a parsed representation with exact bytes. B overlooks the two added carriage returns. D invents a cause and assigns a separate synthetic transformation to C09. The preserved representation and its documented derivative remain different objects.
questions.source: Chapter 4, Week 4 / course Day 18, #week-04-day-03, Offline W4-BYTES control and executed output; EX018 worked representation control.

questions.prompt: C4X labels a declaration checked=True with digest text sha256:toy. What does that program actually validate?

options.text: An actual digest was recomputed over a received source export.
The declared receipt-state rules; it neither hashes nor authenticates source bytes.
The case's handling satisfies every chain-of-custody requirement.
The two C09 rows exhaust the producer's relevant events.

questions.explanation: B respects the program's explicit scope: it classifies supplied flags and strings, not actual collection or hashing. A invents a computation absent from the listing. C extrapolates a toy state rule to comprehensive custody or admissibility. D confuses a receipt-state declaration with source completeness. The missing-digest control remains unverified even when checked=True.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.E6, C4X environment and interpretation; Week 4 / course Day 17, #week-04-day-02, Laboratory and decision; EX017.

questions.prompt: C10 displays 11:21 UTC+02:00. Which time annotation preserves both the arithmetic and its evidential limit?

options.text: 13:21 UTC, with backend state therefore confirmed.
11:21 UTC, because a displayed offset must be ignored.
09:21 UTC as an independently verified capture timestamp.
Conditional 09:21 UTC; retain the raw display and unverified clock context.

questions.explanation: D subtracts the stated two-hour offset while retaining the condition that the displayed clock/offset is correct. A adds rather than subtracts and invents authoritative state. B discards the supplied offset. C computes the right digits but wrongly authenticates capture time. The support receipt remains a separate 09:22 case event.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.9; Week 4 / course Day 19, #week-04-day-04, Theory and mechanism and C10 arithmetic; EX019.

questions.prompt: C10's conditional displayed UTC time is 09:21 and its case receipt is 09:22. What does the one-minute difference measure?

options.text: No verified capture-to-receipt latency; the displayed clock's meaning and accuracy are unestablished.
Exactly one minute of network transfer latency.
Exactly one minute of authoritative S42 unavailability.
The time since the database slot last changed.

questions.explanation: A distinguishes arithmetic between labels from a measurement with validated start and end points. B invents a network start time and transfer measurement. C invents service-duration evidence. D treats a display time as a backend transition record. Capture-device clock, displayed-time semantics, page cache and authoritative state all require their own contextual checks.
questions.source: Chapter 4, Week 4 / course Day 19, #week-04-day-04, C10 time comparison and Worked contrast; EX019 worked context annotation.

questions.prompt: A later authorized read returns S42's current value and version. Which additional claim does that result alone fail to establish?

options.text: The read returned the reported current value.
A version was included in that read result.
The authoritative value at the screenshot's claimed historical time was the same.
The current read can inform the present impact assessment.

questions.explanation: C requires historical records and a validated time/state relationship beyond a current read. A and B restate the hypothetical result supplied in the prompt. D is a bounded decision use of a current-state observation, provided its source and read time are retained. A future read must not silently rewrite the earlier screenshot caption or claim an historical transition time.
questions.source: Chapter 4, Week 4 / course Day 19, #week-04-day-04, Decision and limit; Day 20, #week-04-day-05, second request; EX019–EX020.

questions.prompt: C09 reports a case copy received, while C08 reports source expiry at 10:00. What follows about a source-preservation hold?

options.text: The copy receipt automatically proves producer deletion was suspended.
A hold needs its own authority, application and effect evidence; receipt does not establish it.
The reported deadline authorizes a tenant-wide export without another decision.
A matching local checksum would prove the source cannot expire.

questions.explanation: B keeps the source-preservation control ledger separate from the collected-item custody ledger. A treats a retained copy as proof of producer-side retention. C expands a reported loss warning into permission. D substitutes byte consistency for a hold mechanism and its observed effect. The next work is a bounded custodian request under actual scope, not an invented hold or automatic evidence-loss prevention.
questions.source: Chapter 4, §4.E3; Week 4 / course Day 20, #week-04-day-05, loss-risk and review/stop paragraphs; EX020.
